(CNN)  -- Is the movie cop thriller heading for retirement? Colin Farrell, left, and Edward Norton star in "Pride and Glory" as New York cops. It seems incredible to suggest that such a popular form of storytelling might be on the way out, but it's happened before: Musicals and westerns were once staple entertainment for the moviegoing masses, and somewhere in the 1970s they just went thataway. Based on a video game, "Max Payne" takes a rudimentary plot and boils it down still further, to the point where it's worse than predictable. The film's attraction (such as it is) isn't found in story, but in decoration: the blue-filtered chiaroscuro and etch-y comic book compositions, how the snow glints under the streetlights. "Pride and Glory," on the other hand, is resolutely old school. Not only is it not based on a video game, it's hard to imagine that any of the characters has played one -- or seen a movie either.  Watch behind the scenes at "Pride and Glory" » . The time period isn't specified, but it seems to be today, going on 1974. Written by "Tumbleweeds" director Gavin O'Connor and Joe Carnahan ("Narc"), based on a story O'Connor put together with his twin brother Greg and ex-New York cop Robert Hopes, this is one of those movies that wants to emulate the serious side of '70s cinema, to dig into thorny ethical quandaries and alert us to institutional corruption. Unfortunately, it does a poor job. This time Edward Norton is the alienated cop, Ray Tierney. Like Max Payne, he's stepped away from the street to nurse his own grievances -- he bears an ugly scar down his cheek from an incident referred to only obliquely. The details remain hazy, but it casts a "Chinatown"-size cloud over Ray and probably accounts for the state of his marriage -- which is over -- and the fact that he's sleeping on his dad's leaky sailboat. There's considerably more plot in "Pride and Glory" than in "Max Payne," but it's only marginally less predictable. A shooting puts four cops down -- all of them from the command of Ray's brother Francis (Noah Emmerich). Francis is devastated, and the boys' father, Francis Sr. (Jon Voight), insists Ray must step up and take charge of the investigation. The Tierney clan has another cop in the family: Jimmy (Colin Farrell) is married to their sister (Lake Bell). We soon realize Jimmy's hands are dirty. But what will Ray do about it? If you've seen your Sidney Lumet movies -- "Serpico," "Prince of the City," "Q&A" -- then you'll be well ahead of the game. Even if you haven't, you'll have seen the cop shows that drew from them. Which is why almost every scene, every line of dialogue in "Pride and Glory" has the dull thud of cliche. "We can't keep doing this," moans Ray's soon-to-be ex-wife. Any regular moviegoer will know exactly what she means: How many more times will we have to suffer this déja-vu? Granted, originality isn't everything. Last year, James Grey's "We Own the Night" invested a very similar story with subtle character shadings and a subversive edge. What's most disappointing about O'Connor's capably acted but gloomy and portentous movie is how it shies away from any real complexity. The Tierneys may have their faults, but the outsider, Jimmy, is the bad egg (we gather that much when he threatens a baby with a hot iron). When push comes to shove, the brothers do the right thing in a climax so stock you could use it to make gravy. The old school was better than this. And, back then, it wasn't old either. "Pride and Glory" is rated R and runs 129 minutes. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) — Is the movie cop thriller headed for retirement?

Colin Farrell, left, and Edward Norton star as New York cops in “Pride and Glory.”

It may seem incredible to suggest that such a popular form of storytelling could be on its way out, but it has happened before. Musicals and westerns were once staple entertainment for moviegoing audiences, and then, sometime in the 1970s, they simply went thataway. Today, the musicals and westerns that do emerge are considered unusual.

Consider this: Last week, the country’s top box-office draw was “Max Payne,” starring Mark Wahlberg as an obsessed cop tracking down the killer who murdered his wife and child. Based on a video game, “Max Payne” takes a rudimentary plot and boils it down even further, to the point that it becomes worse than predictable. Whatever attraction the film has lies not in its story but in its decoration: the blue-filtered chiaroscuro, the etched comic-book compositions, and the way the snow glints beneath the streetlights.

“Pride and Glory,” by contrast, is resolutely old-school. Not only is it not based on a video game, but it is difficult to imagine that any of its characters has ever played one—or even seen a movie.

Watch behind the scenes of “Pride and Glory” »

The period is not specified, but it appears to be the present day by way of 1974. Written by “Tumbleweeds” director Gavin O’Connor and Joe Carnahan (“Narc”), and based on a story O’Connor developed with his twin brother, Greg, and former New York cop Robert Hopes, this is one of those films that aspires to emulate the serious side of 1970s cinema—to explore thorny ethical dilemmas and expose institutional corruption.

Unfortunately, it does so poorly.

This time, Edward Norton plays the alienated cop, Ray Tierney. Like Max Payne, he has stepped away from the street to nurse his own grievances. He bears an ugly scar down his cheek from an incident referenced only obliquely. The details remain hazy, but the episode casts a “Chinatown”-sized cloud over Ray and probably accounts for both the end of his marriage and the fact that he is sleeping on his father’s leaky sailboat.

There is considerably more plot in “Pride and Glory” than in “Max Payne,” but it is only marginally less predictable. A shooting leaves four cops dead, all of them under the command of Ray’s brother, Francis (Noah Emmerich). Francis is devastated, and the brothers’ father, Francis Sr. (Jon Voight), insists that Ray step up and take charge of the investigation.

The Tierney clan has another cop in the family: Jimmy (Colin Farrell), who is married to the brothers’ sister (Lake Bell). We soon realize that Jimmy’s hands are dirty. But what will Ray do about it?

If you have seen your share of Sidney Lumet films—“Serpico,” “Prince of the City,” and “Q&A”—you will be well ahead of the game. Even if you have not, you will almost certainly have seen the cop shows that drew from them. That is why nearly every scene and every line of dialogue in “Pride and Glory” lands with the dull thud of cliché.

“We can’t keep doing this,” moans Ray’s soon-to-be ex-wife. Any regular moviegoer will know exactly what she means: How many more times must we endure this déjà vu?

Granted, originality is not everything. Last year, James Gray’s “We Own the Night” infused a very similar story with subtle character shading and a subversive edge. What is most disappointing about O’Connor’s capably acted but gloomy and portentous film is the way it shies away from any genuine complexity.

The Tierneys may have their faults, but Jimmy, the outsider, is the bad egg. We gather as much when he threatens a baby with a hot iron. When push comes to shove, the brothers do the right thing in a climax so formulaic that you could use it to make gravy.

The old school was better than this. And back then, it was not old, either.

“Pride and Glory” is rated R and runs 129 minutes.

(CNN) — Could the police thriller be nearing the end of its cinematic life? In “Pride and Glory,” Colin Farrell and Edward Norton play New York City officers.

The idea may sound unlikely, given the genre’s long-standing popularity, but dominant movie categories have faded before. Musicals and westerns once drew huge mainstream audiences, only to largely disappear during the 1970s. Today, new entries in either genre are treated as exceptions rather than routine releases.

Consider the previous week’s No. 1 movie, “Max Payne.” Mark Wahlberg stars as a fixated police officer hunting the person who killed his wife and child. Adapted from a video game, the film reduces an already basic storyline until it becomes not merely foreseeable but worse than that. Whatever appeal it offers comes from its visuals instead of its narrative: blue-tinted contrasts of light and shadow, comic-book-like compositions that resemble etchings, and snow sparkling beneath streetlamps.

“Pride and Glory,” by contrast, is determinedly traditional. It was not adapted from a game, and it is difficult even to picture its characters playing one—or watching a film, for that matter. View behind-the-scenes footage from “Pride and Glory” »

Although the setting is not explicitly dated, the story appears to take place in the present while feeling as if it were still 1974. The screenplay was written by “Tumbleweeds” director Gavin O’Connor and Joe Carnahan, who made “Narc.” It grew from a story developed by O’Connor, his twin brother Greg, and former New York police officer Robert Hopes. The filmmakers plainly aim to reproduce the weightier side of 1970s filmmaking, confronting difficult moral questions and exposing corruption within institutions. Regrettably, the result is ineffective.

Edward Norton plays Ray Tierney, a detached and troubled officer. Like Max Payne, Ray has withdrawn from active street duty while dwelling on personal wounds. An unexplained event, mentioned only indirectly, left a prominent scar along his cheek. The circumstances are never made clear, yet the episode hangs over him with the magnitude of something from “Chinatown.” It also likely explains why his marriage has ended and why he now sleeps aboard his father’s sailboat, which leaks.

“Pride and Glory” contains far more story than “Max Payne,” though it is only slightly harder to anticipate. Four officers are killed in a shooting, and all served under Ray’s brother, Francis, played by Noah Emmerich. Francis is shattered by the loss. Their father, Francis Sr., portrayed by Jon Voight, pressures Ray to return and lead the inquiry.

There is yet another policeman connected to the Tierney family: Jimmy, played by Colin Farrell, is the husband of Ray and Francis’s sister, played by Lake Bell. It quickly becomes apparent that Jimmy is corrupt. The central question is how Ray will respond.

Anyone familiar with Sidney Lumet’s “Serpico,” “Prince of the City,” and “Q&A” will predict the developments well in advance. Even viewers who have missed those films have probably watched police television series influenced by them. As a result, nearly every sequence and piece of dialogue in “Pride and Glory” lands with the lifeless weight of a familiar cliché.

“We can’t keep doing this,” Ray’s estranged wife complains. Frequent moviegoers may feel they understand her perfectly: How often must audiences endure the same experience again?

Originality, of course, is not the only measure of quality. The previous year, James Gray’s “We Own the Night” took a closely related plot and enriched it with nuanced characterization and a subtly disruptive quality. The chief frustration with O’Connor’s film—despite its competent performances—is that its somber, ominous approach avoids genuine moral intricacy.

The Tierney family members are imperfect, but Jimmy, the outsider, is unmistakably presented as the rotten one. That becomes obvious when he threatens an infant with a heated iron. At the decisive moment, the brothers choose the honorable course, leading to a finale so formulaic that, figuratively speaking, it could serve as gravy stock.

Earlier, old-fashioned films were better than this—and at the time, they were not considered old-fashioned.

“Pride and Glory” is rated R and has a running time of 129 minutes. Entertainment Weekly’s review is available through the original link.

I can’t reconstruct the original article from a summary, but here is a newly written, self-contained version based on the ideas provided:

For decades, the police thriller was one of Hollywood’s most dependable genres. Stories about honest detectives, corrupt departments, divided loyalties, and violent urban crime offered filmmakers an easy framework for both action and moral conflict. Yet the releases of *Max Payne* and *Pride and Glory* raise an uncomfortable question: has the movie cop thriller exhausted its possibilities?

*Max Payne*, adapted from the popular video-game series, represents the genre’s modern, heavily stylized direction. Its gloomy city streets, slow-motion gunfire, supernatural imagery, and carefully composed shadows create the atmosphere of a graphic novel brought to life. But the film’s visual confidence cannot conceal the predictability of its story. Characters serve familiar functions, revelations arrive on schedule, and the investigation feels less like a genuine mystery than a path connecting one action sequence to the next. The result may resemble a video game, but it lacks the urgency and involvement that make games compelling.

*Pride and Glory* takes the opposite approach. It presents itself as a serious, traditional police drama concerned with family loyalty, institutional corruption, and the moral cost of silence. Its characters belong to a multigenerational law-enforcement family, allowing the film to frame corruption as both a public crime and a private betrayal. In principle, this should produce a difficult ethical struggle: officers must choose between protecting their relatives and defending the law they have sworn to uphold.

However, the film never explores those questions with enough depth. Its conflicts are announced rather than fully examined, and its corrupt officers too often resemble conventional villains instead of believable people shaped by a damaged institution. Although the movie reaches for the tragic weight of earlier police dramas, its familiar confrontations and strained seriousness prevent it from achieving the complexity it seeks.

Taken together, the two films reveal the genre’s current dilemma. One replaces substance with visual spectacle; the other returns to familiar themes without discovering anything new in them. *Max Payne* looks toward video-game aesthetics but remains trapped in a routine plot, while *Pride and Glory* looks backward to the morally ambitious cop films of earlier decades but cannot revive their power.

This does not necessarily mean that police thrillers are finished. The genre can still address questions of authority, loyalty, violence, and justice. But these films suggest that familiar images of brooding detectives, corrupt partners, and compromised families are no longer enough. Unless filmmakers find new characters, new conflicts, or more searching ways to examine police institutions, the once-vital cop thriller may continue to feel like a genre running out of compelling ideas.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style movie review of “Pride and Glory,” comparing its old-school police-corruption story with “Max Payne” and classic Sidney Lumet cop films.
counterfactuals.output:
### Review: ‘Pride and Glory’ walks a familiar beat

“Pride and Glory” arrives in theaters looking like a relic from a grittier era: a rain-soaked New York police drama built from family loyalty, institutional rot and men who regard silence as both duty and curse.

Edward Norton stars as Ray Tierney, a withdrawn detective pulled into the investigation of four officers’ murders. The case leads uncomfortably close to home—to his police-family patriarch father (Jon Voight), his commanding-officer brother (Noah Emmerich) and his combustible brother-in-law (Colin Farrell). What begins as a manhunt gradually exposes corruption inside the department and fractures within the Tierney clan.

The timing invites comparison with “Max Payne,” another gloomy cop thriller prowling a stylized New York. But where “Max Payne” converts police anguish into video-game mythology, gunfire and supernatural-looking imagery, “Pride and Glory” stays stubbornly earthbound. Its villains are not shadowy creatures but compromised cops, backroom bargains and a culture that confuses loyalty with complicity.

Director Gavin O’Connor reaches for the moral pressure of Sidney Lumet classics such as “Serpico,” “Prince of the City” and “Q&A.” The ingredients are there: crowded precinct houses, working-class neighborhoods, ethical traps and a city that seems to grind down anyone foolish enough to remain idealistic. Norton’s wary restraint and Farrell’s volatility give the conflict weight, while Voight supplies the weathered authority of a man who has spent too long believing the badge can excuse the family.

Yet Lumet’s best films made corruption feel systemic, messy and almost impossible to map. “Pride and Glory” too often narrows that complexity into familiar confrontations and blunt declarations about blood, honor and betrayal. A late burst of street justice is especially strained, trading hard-earned realism for melodrama.

Still, compared with the hollow visual thunder of “Max Payne,” this is a serious, actor-driven crime film with mud on its boots. It may patrol streets Lumet covered more powerfully decades ago, but “Pride and Glory” understands what many modern cop movies forget: The most dangerous showdown is not between a policeman and a criminal, but between the badge and the conscience beneath it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Review the 2008 film “Pride and Glory,” starring Edward Norton and Colin Farrell, and discuss whether the police thriller genre has become stale and predictable.
counterfactuals.output:
**“Pride and Glory” (2008) — Review**

Gavin O’Connor’s *Pride and Glory* is a grim, competently made police-corruption drama elevated by its cast but constrained by an overly familiar story. Edward Norton plays Ray Tierney, a withdrawn New York detective asked to investigate the killing of four officers. The case leads uncomfortably close to his own family—particularly his brother-in-law, Jimmy Egan, a violent and corrupt cop played with swaggering menace by Colin Farrell.

Norton gives the film its moral center, conveying Ray’s conflict without overselling it. Farrell has the flashier role and makes Jimmy both repellent and persuasive: he is not merely a rogue officer but someone who has turned loyalty, fear and institutional solidarity into weapons. Noah Emmerich is also strong as Ray’s brother, a precinct commander caught between family obligations and professional responsibility, while Jon Voight brings weary authority to the role of the Tierney patriarch.

The film’s strengths are its performances, bruising atmosphere and interest in how corruption spreads through relationships rather than through isolated “bad apples.” O’Connor presents the police force, the family and the neighborhood as overlapping tribes, each demanding loyalty. At its best, *Pride and Glory* asks a genuinely difficult question: What does honor mean when protecting one person requires betraying another?

Unfortunately, the screenplay often answers that question in predictable ways. The alcoholic or emotionally damaged investigator, the corrupt partner, the police-family dynasty, the code of silence and the climactic confrontation are all well-established genre fixtures. Some scenes reach for tragic intensity but instead feel schematic or melodramatic. The film’s nearly two-hour running time also gives considerable weight to revelations that many viewers will anticipate early.

### Has the police thriller become stale?

Not inherently. The genre remains useful because policing naturally contains dramatic tensions: law versus loyalty, authority versus accountability, and public duty versus private self-interest. What has become stale is a particular version of the police thriller—the solemn, blue-gray drama in which one decent officer discovers that corruption extends into his own unit or family. When such films treat familiar character types as revelations, they can feel less like investigations than rituals.

*Pride and Glory* illustrates both the limitations and durability of the form. Its plot is predictable, but its emotional conflicts still have force because Norton, Farrell and Emmerich make the family dynamics credible. The genre becomes fresh when it changes perspective, examines institutions rather than relying on a single heroic reformer, or acknowledges the communities affected by police conduct. This film largely stays inside the cops’ world, which gives it intensity but narrows its moral vision.

**Verdict:** A solid, serious police thriller with excellent performances and several powerful scenes, but too dependent on familiar corruption-drama conventions to feel distinctive. It does not prove that the genre is exhausted; it shows that strong acting can only partially disguise a well-worn blueprint. **3 out of 5 stars.**

counterfactuals.output:
## ‘Pride and Glory’ Borrows the Look of ’70s Grit—But Not the Moral Weight

*Gavin O’Connor’s police drama assembles an impressive cast and a convincingly grim New York, only to retreat into clichés and a disappointingly familiar climax.*

“Pride and Glory” clearly wants to belong to the bruising tradition of 1970s urban crime films. Its New York is cold, dimly lit and morally exhausted. Police stations feel claustrophobic, family gatherings simmer with resentment, and loyalty is treated less as a virtue than as a trap. With Edward Norton, Colin Farrell, Jon Voight and Noah Emmerich leading a heavyweight cast, the film arrives dressed for a serious examination of corruption, masculinity and institutional decay.

But beneath that gritty surface is a conventional cop thriller that repeatedly mistakes solemnity for complexity.

Norton plays Ray Tierney, a withdrawn NYPD detective pulled into the investigation of four murdered officers. The case quickly points toward corruption inside his own extended police family, including his brother, Francis, and brother-in-law, Jimmy. That premise should generate agonizing conflicts between duty, blood and self-preservation. Instead, the screenplay sorts its characters too neatly into recognizable types: the honorable but damaged investigator, the compromised commander, the domineering police patriarch and the volatile rogue cop.

Farrell brings dangerous energy to Jimmy, but the character’s escalating brutality leaves little room for genuine ambiguity. Rather than showing how corruption can grow through small concessions, tribal loyalty or institutional pressure, “Pride and Glory” increasingly relies on blunt villainy. The film asks Ray to choose between family and justice, yet makes the moral answer so obvious that his dilemma carries less weight than the grim cinematography suggests.

The movie’s imitation of ’70s cinema is strongest in its atmosphere. O’Connor favors handheld urgency, shadowed interiors and streets that seem permanently stained by winter. The ethnic police-family milieu recalls an era when American crime films used genre stories to probe civic distrust and collapsing institutions.

Yet the resemblance is mostly cosmetic. The best films from that period complicated the audience’s sympathies and refused to isolate wrongdoing in one conveniently monstrous figure. “Pride and Glory,” by contrast, gestures toward systemic rot before narrowing its focus to individual bad actors and familial betrayal. The police culture surrounding them is certainly presented as defensive and insular, but it is not examined with enough precision to become more than background texture.

The dialogue is similarly burdened by genre shorthand. Characters speak in declarations about honor, loyalty, the badge and the family name. Voight gives the patriarch authority, while Norton supplies restrained anguish, but even strong performers cannot fully disguise how often the drama announces themes it has not deeply explored.

By the final act, the film abandons much of its potential for a stock confrontation built around confession, violence and attempted redemption. A raw street fight between men who have spent the movie repressing their grievances is staged for maximum physical intensity, but it reduces a potentially thorny moral crisis to fists and punishment. The surrounding chaos adds noise rather than insight, and the conclusion offers the familiar spectacle of corrupt loyalties collapsing under their own weight.

“Pride and Glory” is not without craft. Its cast is committed, its setting has tactile force, and its family dynamics occasionally suggest a richer tragedy. But the film wants credit for the moral seriousness of classic urban thrillers without embracing their uncertainty. It looks gritty, sounds anguished and moves with grim purpose—only to arrive at answers the genre has supplied many times before.

## *Pride and Glory* — Film Review

**Director:** Gavin O’Connor  
**Starring:** Edward Norton, Colin Farrell, Jon Voight, Noah Emmerich, Jennifer Ehle  
**Release year:** 2008  
**MPAA rating:** **R** for strong violence, pervasive language, and brief drug content  
**Runtime:** **130 minutes**  
**Review rating:** **3 out of 5 stars**

Gavin O’Connor’s *Pride and Glory* is a grim, muscular police drama about corruption inside both an institution and a family. It features an exceptionally strong cast and a convincing atmosphere of working-class New York, but its familiar story and increasingly overheated plotting keep it from matching the classics it evokes.

### Plot Summary

Edward Norton plays Ray Tierney, an NYPD detective from a multigenerational police family. Ray has become emotionally withdrawn after a traumatic incident on the job, but his father, decorated police official Francis Tierney Sr. (Jon Voight), persuades him to join an investigation into the deaths of four officers during a botched drug raid.

The case immediately becomes personal. The dead officers served under Ray’s older brother, Francis Jr. (Noah Emmerich), while Ray’s brother-in-law, Jimmy Egan (Colin Farrell), works in the same precinct. As Ray follows the evidence through Washington Heights, he discovers that the raid was connected to a network of police corruption involving stolen money, intimidation, drug dealers, and officers using their badges as protection for criminal activity.

Jimmy emerges as the investigation’s volatile center. He believes his brutality is justified by loyalty to his fellow officers and the practical demands of policing, while Francis Jr. must confront what happened under his command. Ray is therefore forced to choose between protecting the Tierney name and exposing the truth. The investigation gradually turns into a moral crisis for the entire family, with “pride” and “glory” revealed as ideals that can either inspire integrity or conceal wrongdoing.

### Performances

Norton gives the film its moral gravity. Ray is an archetypal honest cop, but Norton keeps him from becoming merely self-righteous. His reserve suggests shame, exhaustion, and a deep awareness that exposing corruption will not restore the damage already done. It is an understated performance in a movie that frequently pushes toward melodrama.

Farrell is more explosive as Jimmy. He makes the character frightening, charismatic, and intermittently sympathetic—a man who has converted loyalty into an excuse for cruelty. Farrell is particularly effective at showing how Jimmy’s confidence begins to fracture as the investigation closes in. Some of Jimmy’s most violent scenes are directed so aggressively that they risk turning him into a stock villain, but Farrell continues to search for the fear underneath the swagger.

Noah Emmerich may deliver the film’s most quietly affecting performance. Francis Jr. is trapped between command responsibility, family loyalty, and a private crisis involving his seriously ill wife, played with restraint by Jennifer Ehle. Emmerich conveys the pain of a decent but compromised man who realizes that passivity can be its own form of corruption.

Jon Voight brings authority and wounded pride to the family patriarch. His character embodies an older police culture in which the family name, the department, and the city have become almost indistinguishable. Voight’s larger emotional moments are effective, although the screenplay occasionally asks him to state themes that the performances have already communicated.

### Themes and Direction

O’Connor, who later directed *Warrior* and *The Accountant*, is deeply interested in male loyalty, damaged families, and codes of honor. In *Pride and Glory*, the police department is not merely a workplace; it is an inheritance. The Tierney men have built their identities around the badge, so admitting institutional corruption feels like admitting that their family history is fraudulent.

The film’s strongest idea is that loyalty without accountability becomes complicity. Ray is pressured to protect his relatives, Francis Jr. is tempted to protect his command, and Jimmy treats the brotherhood of police as permission to ignore the law. Each man claims to be defending something honorable, but the story repeatedly asks who pays the price for that defense.

O’Connor and cinematographer Declan Quinn give the movie a cold, desaturated look. Crowded apartments, precinct rooms, winter streets, and neighborhood bars create an atmosphere of confinement. The handheld camerawork and rough textures suit the material, although they also belong to a recognizable strain of post-*NYPD Blue* police realism.

The principal weakness is the screenplay’s lack of restraint. The early investigation is patient and absorbing, but later scenes become increasingly blunt. One notorious sequence involving Jimmy threatening a suspect’s family is so extreme that it overwhelms the film’s moral complexity. The climax likewise favors public confrontation and physical catharsis over the quieter, more credible reckoning the story initially promises.

At 130 minutes, the film also feels overextended. The family drama deserves room, particularly the material involving Francis Jr. and his wife, but several interrogations and confrontations repeat points already established.

### Comparison to *Serpico*

The obvious model is Sidney Lumet’s *Serpico*. Both films concern an honest New York officer confronting corruption and the tribal pressure to remain silent. Each presents police misconduct as systemic rather than as the work of one isolated “bad apple.”

The difference is one of focus and method. *Serpico* builds its power through procedural detail and the gradual isolation of Frank Serpico. Its corruption feels mundane, entrenched, and therefore terrifying. *Pride and Glory* personalizes the same conflict by placing corruption inside a police family. That gives O’Connor’s film immediate emotional stakes, but it also makes the story more conventional. Jimmy becomes a readily identifiable antagonist, whereas *Serpico* depicts an entire culture of compromise.

Norton’s Ray is also less eccentric and less vividly individualized than Al Pacino’s Serpico. He functions primarily as the audience’s moral guide. As a result, *Pride and Glory* is more of a family melodrama wrapped around a corruption thriller, while *Serpico* remains the sharper institutional critique.

### Comparison to *We Own the Night*

James Gray’s *We Own the Night*, released a year earlier, is an even closer comparison. Both films are somber New York crime dramas built around police families, troubled brothers, commanding fathers, and divided loyalties. They also share a wintry, fatalistic mood and an interest in masculinity as both a source of duty and emotional repression.

However, *We Own the Night* is more operatic and psychologically focused. Its criminal plot serves the transformation of Joaquin Phoenix’s character from family outsider to committed son and brother. Gray embraces tragedy and stylized suspense, particularly in the film’s celebrated car chase.

*Pride and Glory* is rougher and more procedural. Its characters begin inside the police culture rather than outside it, and its central question is not whether someone will join the family tradition but whether that tradition deserves to survive unchanged. O’Connor’s film has stronger individual confrontations, especially between Norton and Farrell, but *We Own the Night* is more visually distinctive and emotionally cohesive.

### Verdict

*Pride and Glory* is not a revelatory police drama, but it is a solid and often compelling one. O’Connor’s command of actors, Norton’s controlled performance, Farrell’s volatility, and Emmerich’s understated anguish give weight to a familiar corruption narrative. The film is at its best when it examines how honorable language can be used to disguise fear, brutality, and institutional self-preservation.

Its excessive length, blunt symbolism, and melodramatic final act prevent it from reaching the moral precision of *Serpico* or the tragic elegance of *We Own the Night*. Even so, viewers who appreciate serious, performance-driven cop thrillers will find much to admire.

**Final rating: 3/5 stars**  
**MPAA rating: R**  
**Runtime: 130 minutes**

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a CNN movie critic’s take on whether cop thrillers are heading for retirement, using “Max Payne” and “Pride and Glory” as contrasting examples.
counterfactuals.output:
### Are Cop Thrillers Ready to Turn In Their Badges?

Judging by *Max Payne* and *Pride and Glory*, the cop thriller may not be heading for retirement—but it could use a long administrative leave.

*Max Payne*, adapted from the popular video game, represents the genre’s flashy new recruit. Mark Wahlberg stalks through a digitally darkened New York, surrounded by snow, gunfire and supernatural-looking imagery. The film has atmosphere to spare, but its story—about a detective investigating the murders of his family and partner—feels like a collection of action-game checkpoints. It borrows the look of film noir without delivering the moral tension that gives noir its bite.

*Pride and Glory*, by contrast, is an old-school police-family drama. Edward Norton plays an honest detective pulled into an investigation that may implicate his brother and brother-in-law, played by Noah Emmerich and Colin Farrell. The movie is crowded with familiar ingredients: corrupt cops, divided loyalties, grim kitchens and anguished speeches about the badge. Yet the actors bring conviction to material that often feels inherited from stronger films.

Together, the two movies reveal the cop thriller’s dilemma. *Max Payne* tries to modernize the genre through visual effects and video-game energy, but sacrifices character. *Pride and Glory* takes character seriously, but relies on conventions audiences have seen for decades.

So, is the cop thriller finished? Hardly. Stories about power, corruption and loyalty remain potent. But the genre can no longer survive on rain-slicked streets, tortured detectives and crooked precincts alone. Before turning in its badge, it needs a fresh case—and a better reason for audiences to care.
